📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Hollywood Reporter announced Wednesday that award-winning writer, director, actor and producer Mindy Kaling will receive this year’s Equity in Entertainment Award during its annual Women in Entertainment breakfast gala in Los Angeles.

Recent findings suggest that actor Maitreyi Ramakrishnan, who starred in Kaling’s hit Netflix series Never Have I Ever, will present Kaling with the award. Kaling joins Taylor Swift, who The Hollywood Reporter previously announced will receive the Sherry Lansing Leadership Award, as an honoree at this year’s gala. Related Stories General News Taylor Swift Will Be Honored With The Hollywood Reporter's Sherry Lansing Leadership Award at Women in Entertainment Gala News Black Lives Matter Activist DeRay Mckesson Talks Losing Key Trump-Era Protest Mobilization Tool: "I Miss Twitter".

According to recent reports, additionally, actress and comedian Mary Beth Barone is set to open the program, which is presented by founding sponsor Lifetime and title sponsor Lilly. Lina Polimeni, chief marketing officer — consumer at Eli Lilly and Firm, will share remarks on the vital intersection of health and entertainment.

The Equity in Entertainment Award recognizes individuals who amplify the voices of underrepresented communities in the entertainment industry. The award was created in 2016, and previous honorees include Jennifer Lopez, Selena Gomez, Kerry Washington, Issa Rae, Ryan Murphy, Amy Pascal and Nina Jacobson.

Recent findings suggest that “Mindy Kaling is one of the most influential creative voices of her generation,” stated Maer Roshan, editor-in-chief of The Hollywood Reporter. “Through her sharp humor, emotional honesty and inclusive storytelling, Kaling creates opportunities for latest perspectives and stories to take center stage. We’re thrilled to recognize her with this year’s Equity in Entertainment Award, celebrating her enduring contributions to the industry and her commitment to making entertainment more inclusive and reflective of the world we live in.”.

Kaling is an Emmy-nominated writer, Tony Award-winning producer, Latest York Times best-selling author, acclaimed director and actor. At age 24, Kaling joined the writing staff of NBC’s The Office, becoming the only woman on the team. She penned 23 episodes over eight seasons, which was more than any other writer. Kaling also earned an Emmy nomination, marking the first time a woman of color had been recognized in any writing category.

Her achievements have continued to garner national recognition. In 2023, Kaling was awarded the National Medal of Arts by the White House, the highest honor bestowed upon artists by the U.S. government, and received the Producers Guild of America’s Norman Lear Achievement Award in Television. She has been named to Time’s 100 Most Influential People in the World list (2012), and in 2022, her tech giant, Kaling International, was named one of Time’s 100 Most Influential Companies.

Kaling is the creator, star and executive producer of the hit series The Mindy Project, for which she wrote 24 of the show’s 117 episodes over six celebrated seasons. Since then, she has solidified her reputation as one of Hollywood’s most prolific and powerful storytellers, particularly in shaping the future of comedy, teen drama and women-led television.

Industry observers note that in 2020, she created the Netflix teen dramedy Never Have I Ever, which reached 40 million households in its first four weeks and concluded in 2023 to widespread acclaim. She co-created and executive produced The Sex Lives of College Girls, which became the most watched comedy premiere on Max in 2021. In 2024, she produced the Oscar-nominated short film Anuja, a powerful narrative about sisterhood, exploitation and hope.

In 2025, Kaling co-created and executive produced Running Point for Netflix, which debuted as the No. 1 TV show in the U.S., surpassing a billion minutes viewed in its first week. The series was quickly renewed for a second season, which recently premiered on Netflix. She is also the creator and executive producer of the 2026 Hulu series Not Suitable for Work, a workplace dramedy following a group of ambitious young professionals in Manhattan.

It has been revealed that through her organization, Kaling International, she has cultivated a distinctive brand rooted in sharp humor, emotional honesty and inclusive storytelling. Her leadership has helped launch the careers of diverse new writers, showrunners and creatives, particularly women and people of color who have gone on to shape major projects across the industry.

Beyond television and film, Kaling is a best-selling author. Her comedic memoirs Is Everyone Hanging Out Without Me? (And Other Concerns) and Why Not Me? became Newly introduced York Times best-sellers, followed by her personal essay collection Nothing Like I Imagined. She went on to launch Mindy’s Book Studio in partnership with Amazon Publishing, an imprint dedicated to championing new and underrepresented literary voices. In January 2027, Kaling will release I Did Everything Right, Right?, a collection of six personal essays from Amazon Original Stories exploring motherhood, ambition, identity and the unexpected realities of adulthood with her signature wit and candor.

According to recent reports, polimeni will speak about the need for more accurate depictions of breast cancer onscreen. She will cite research, funded by Lilly and conducted with Dr. Stacy Smith and the USC Annenberg Inclusion Initiative, finding that just two female characters had breast cancer across a full year of Hollywood’s most popular films and TV highlights, out of more than 8,600 speaking characters. Polimeni will urge the industry to bring more stories to screen that reflect the experiences of women living with breast cancer. Her remarks come as Lilly brings free mobile mammograms to Koreatown in Los Angeles from Dec. 4-6, a neighborhood with one of the densest concentrations of late-stage breast cancer diagnoses in L.A. County, so more women can get screened close to home.

It has been revealed that ramakrishnan first captured the attention of international audiences as the charmingly relatable Devi Vishwakumar in Netflix’s hit series Never Have I Ever and has shifted into high gear ever since. She leads Netflix’s comedy dance film Best of the Best, now streaming. Other recent projects include scene-stealing as Lindsay Lohan’s endearingly neurotic pop star client Ella in Disney’s Freakier Friday and in Amy Wang’s horror-comedy Slanted. She has also guest starred in Prime Video’s critically acclaimed series The Boys as Countess Crow and has voiced characters in witty coming-of-age stories including Netflix’s Major Mouth and Disney’s Turning Red. Up next, she has roles in The Angry Birds Movie 3, in theaters Dec. 23, and season two of Prime Video’s Legally Blonde prequel series Elle, expected to release next year.

According to recent reports, barone is a comedian, writer, actor and producer. She recently wrapped production on the independent film Still We Met, which Barone wrote and stars in opposite Joe Alwyn. Barone’s original series Hard Feelings, which she created, wrote and will lead, was recently acquired by Hulu and A24. She also stars in and writes for the hit Amazon and A24 comedy series Overcompensating, which will return for a second season Feb. 17, 2027. Barone recently wrapped production on the Amazon MGM Studios romantic comedy Love Love, in which she will appear opposite Tyriq Withers and Isabel May. Her hourlong comedy special, Galaxy Brain, was released on Netflix in July 2026 and made the Netflix Top 10 the week of its release. Galaxy Brain was also released as a comedy album on Aug. 19 and as a limited edition vinyl this fall via Universal Music’s MCA. Barone is the co-host of the popular podcast Ride with Benito Skinner.

Attended by 600 industry leaders and VIPs, THR’s Women in Entertainment breakfast coincides with the release of The Hollywood Reporter’s Women in Entertainment matter, featuring the highly anticipated Power 100, a list of the most powerful female executives and talent in entertainment.

Recent findings suggest that approximately 40 high school juniors and seniors currently participating in THR’s Women in Entertainment Mentorship Program will attend the event. The program pairs some of the brightest young women from underserved high schools across Los Angeles with some of the most powerful female executives in film and TV. The WIE Mentorship Program, now in its 17th year, is a joint venture with Big Brothers Big Sisters of Greater Los Angeles and the Entertainment Industry Foundation. Over 300 students have taken part in the program, with mentees having received more than $16 million in scholarships over the past 17 years. A highlight of the annual breakfast, this year’s celebration will feature the presentation of more than $500,000 in university scholarships to high school seniors in the program, generously provided by The Chuck Lorre Family Foundation and Lifetime. Earlier this month, The Hollywood Reporter declared Target as the newly introduced leading partner of its Women in Entertainment Mentorship Program.

Presented by founding sponsor Lifetime and title sponsor Lilly, THR’s Women in Entertainment event is also sponsored by Delta Air Lines, Target, Waymo and WME and in partnership with Significant Brothers Big Sisters of Greater Los Angeles, Entertainment Industry Foundation, Chapman University, Loyola Marymount University, Golden Goose, UTA Foundation and Warner Bros.

Recent findings suggest that the news comes on the heels of THR’s Daytime Emmys win last month. THR’s acclaimed video roundtable series, Off Script With The Hollywood Reporter, won the award for best arts and popular culture program.

Sources indicate that also in 2026, THR took home a record 20 SoCal Journalism Awards, including best magazine, best website and best podcast — more wins than any other media outlet. It earned a record 96 nominations at the National Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards, outpacing any other press organization, after winning 50 top honors in 2025. Latest Update: Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations.
  • The study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy.
  • Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations. The researchers have found direct experimental evidence that triple bonds involving heavy elements do not always behave according to the familiar rules taught in chemistry classes.

The study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy. In particular, the researchers found that two types of bonds normally treated as distinct can begin to merge, creating a structure that conventional chemistry models do not fully describe.

Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.

"This idea that relativity is notable in heavy elements has been around since the 1970s," noted Lai-Sheng Wang, a professor of chemistry at Brown and the study's corresponding author. "But we show direct spectroscopic evidence that what we learned in high school about chemical bonding isn't true in heavy elements.".

Why Einstein's Relativity Changes Chemical Bonds.

To understand why the discovery matters, it helps to look at how chemical bonds normally form.

Sources indicate that atoms can connect by sharing electrons, the negatively charged particles that surround their positively charged nuclei. In a simple covalent bond, each atom contributes an electron to a shared pair. The attraction between these negatively charged electrons and the two positive nuclei helps hold the atoms together.

Industry observers note that some atoms share multiple pairs of electrons, producing double or triple bonds. According to the standard textbook model, a triple bond consists of three separate connections: one sigma bond and two pi bonds.

The sigma bond is typically the strongest. It forms through a direct, "head-on" overlap of electron orbitals along the axis connecting the two atomic nuclei. The other two connections are pi bonds, which form through weaker, "side-by-side" overlaps on either side of that axis.

In a recent development, for lighter elements, this familiar description works well. However, the situation becomes more complicated farther down the periodic table.

According to recent reports, heavy elements contain nuclei with large numbers of protons, creating powerful electrical attractions that can accelerate nearby electrons to a substantial fraction of the speed of light. At these extreme speeds, effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity become key, changing how the electrons behave.

Recent findings suggest that one particularly important effect is known as spin-orbit coupling. Electrons possess a quantum property called spin, which gives them a magnetic character often described as pointing up or down. Under ordinary conditions, spin and orbital motion can be treated as largely separate properties. But in heavy atoms, relativistic effects can link them strongly together.

That connection changes how electrons interact and disrupts the clear distinction between sigma and pi bonds that traditional chemistry relies on.

In a recent development, "The boundary between a sigma bond and a pi bond is now sort of smeared," Wang remarked. "We still have three bonds, but we don't really strictly have a sigma or a pi anymore.".

Scientists Find Direct Evidence in Bismuth Bonds.

Sources indicate that to test whether this unusual bonding behavior actually occurs, Wang's research group, led by Brown Ph.D. students Deniz Kahraman and Jie Hui, created molecules containing carbon and bismuth.

Bismuth sits next to lead on the periodic table and is among the heavier elements in which relativistic effects are expected to play a major role. That made it an especially useful candidate for investigating whether the familiar rules of triple bonding begin to break down.

Industry observers note that the researchers cooled the molecules to temperatures approaching absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. They then examined the molecules using photoelectron spectroscopy, a technique that uses laser light to eject electrons from molecules.

By measuring the energy of the released electrons, scientists can determine how tightly those electrons were held in place. This provides a detailed picture of the electronic structure responsible for chemical bonding.

The results revealed a striking departure from the conventional model.

Rather than showing the expected combination of one sigma bond and two pi bonds, the carbon-bismuth triple bonds displayed a different arrangement. Their electronic structure was more consistent with one pi bond and two hybrid sigma-pi bonds.

In other words, Einstein's relativity had changed the nature of the chemical connections, blending two traditionally distinct types of bonds into something that standard textbook descriptions do not fully capture.

A Discovery That Could Rewrite Chemistry Textbooks.

Recent findings suggest that the findings provide direct experimental confirmation of relativistic bonding effects that scientists have discussed for decades. Wang believes this evidence could eventually lead to changes in how chemical bonding is explained in chemistry textbooks, particularly as research involving heavy elements continues to expand.

The implications could also extend beyond fundamental chemistry.

It has been revealed that bismuth has attracted growing scientific interest because it may offer a less toxic alternative to lead in next-generation solar cells. Researchers are also exploring its potential in quantum materials and quantum computing, fields that depend on understanding and controlling the behavior of electrons.

A more accurate picture of how heavy atoms form chemical bonds could help scientists investigate these materials and better understand the properties that make them useful for emerging technologies.

"Maybe this will become the upcoming textbook idea as we are dealing with more and more heavy chemistry of the heavy elements," Wang stated.

The research was supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation (CHE-2403841) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-SC0008501).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prime Video's upcoming "Blade Runner 2099" series arrives Nov. 25, 2026, and it flips the cyberpunk universe on its head. The new show casts replicants as the dominant species on Earth, with humans relegated to second-class citizens after a global uprising.

Industry observers note that this dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K. Dick's 1968 novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," and was then so vividly brought to life in Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 adaptation, "Blade Runner." The 2017 sequel, "Blade Runner 2049," was directed by "Arrival’s" and "Dune’s" Denis Villeneuve.

Starring Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer, Matthew Needham, Dimitri Abold, and Lewis Gribben, "Blade Runner 2099" hails from creator and showrunner Silka Louisa and Alcon Entertainment founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, who executive produce with Ridley Scott's Scott Free Productions.

Here, Yeoh's dying replicant blade runner Olwen unites with Schafer’s Cora, a human masquerading as a synthetic, to hunt down a dangerous rogue replicant that holds the key to a dark secret.

We spoke to Kosove and Johnson about being respectful keepers of "Blade Runner's" creative flame, the pitch that sold them, and dipping back into Dick's original novel.

Industry observers note that "When the original film came out in 1982, and even when "2049" came out about a decade ago, a lot of things that these movies envisioned seemed far, far away and hard to comprehend," Kosovo tells Space. "The creation of artificial sentient beings. Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner,' with artificial technology and concerns of how do humans use this technology for our benefit without it taking over.".

"Silka came in several years ago and pitched her very simple idea, which was, the next chapter of 'Blade Runner' should be what happens when the replicants overtake their creators." explains Kosovo.

"We thought that idea was going to be particularly resonant. It was simple to understand so newly introduced fans could enter the world without being steeped in the first two movies. And we thought it had logical continuity to the story canon that came before it. It checked a number of key boxes for us. Even though we talked to a number of showrunners who were much more established in their careers than Silka was at that point, she won the day with the most elegant idea in our opinion.".

Johnson admits that Louisa's pitch approval was just the opening round of a multitude of responsible decisions to be ruminated over as the production process advanced.

Industry observers note that "Once you agree that this is the story we’re telling, then it becomes a multi-year partnership in honoring all the artists and visionaries that came before as it relates to visual design and music," he notes. "Everything needs to be of the highest quality. Even though it's a TV show we feel it has theatrical level visual effects. It’s practical and tactile and analog. There’s a lot of things that come along with how you produce the show. At its core that becomes a partnership when you decide these are the characters I’m going to spend hours with and you go down that journey.".

With nearly 60 years of "Blade Runner" material to play with, there’s bound to be easter eggs dropped into the tale over the course of "Blade Runner 2099's" 8-episode season.

Industry observers note that "You’ve got Tyrell as a critical aspect of our story, but Wallace creeps into the story as well," Kosove teases. "One of the keys things was, from an architectural standpoint, things that exist in "2049" had to exist in this. You see the Wallace spires when you see the Tyrell pyramid. You have the sea wall when they're going south with the spinner.

"There’s some story easter eggs too. Silka did something really cool which has not been done in either movie. She brought in concepts that go back to Philip K. Dick's novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" That was really interesting. We’re really excited for people to see it and see how they respond.”.

"Blade Runner 2099" arrives on Nov. 25, 2026 exclusively on Prime Video.

The U.K.’s harassment and bullying watchdog has seen a spike in whistleblowing reports following Russell Brand’s conviction for rape earlier this month.

It has been revealed that creative Industries Independent Standards Authority, a voluntary body with support across media and the arts, has said it received over 90 reports since launching its whistleblowing service in June, with a spike following Brand’s conviction. The former comedian was sentenced to 10 and a half years in prison after a jury found him guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

The reports cover all the sectors represented by CIISA including film, tv, music, theatre and live performance.

In a recent development, CIISA is an officially designated whistleblowing body and its confidential whistleblowing service is available for those in need of immediate support while enabling it to build up insight. Reports will be used to identify patterns and problems which it can then report back to policymakers and to the industry.

Where necessary, the body will also make “lawful referrals.”.

The news comes as CIISA hosted an event in Parliament Wednesday to engage industry leaders and lawmakers on preventing harmful behaviour in the creative industries. It was hosted by CIISA chair Baroness Helena Kennedy with attendees including numerous MPs, including chair of the digital, culture, media and sport committee Caroline Dinenage as well as media figures such as BBC chair Samir Shah and ex-BBC director general Tim Davie.

Recent findings suggest that the event marked the official launch of CIISA’s register, which displays the organizations financially contributing to CIISA. Orgs supporting the watchdog will be entitled to carry a CIISA registration mark, demonstrating their commitment to the body’s standards, as well as access to events and resources.Contributions are made on a financial sliding scale, with no tech giant expected to pay more than 0.1% of its U.K. turnover.

“CIISA has a pivotal role to play in preventing harm and closing accountability gaps in the creative industry infrastructure, offering a unique opportunity to identify harmful patterns of behaviour across different projects,” noted CIISA CEO Jen Smith.

“We thank the organisations who have already pledged their support for this important work and we will continue to work alongside industry and Government to ensure that CIISA is adequately resourced to offer a safe, confidential route for people to seek independent advice and report concerns, and to embed the consistent cross-sector standards that will drive lasting change.”.
